name: Essential oil blends (massage, aroma, spray or gargle)
short: Case review: harms mild to severe, one death. Case reports: toddler's liver failure after swallowing clove oil; pneumonia after inhaling oils; allergic skin rash. Eczema worsened in children.
text: This entry covers only essential-oil blends massaged into the scalp, skin or abdomen, and oils used as an aroma during sleep or as a spray or gargle; it does not cover the oral terpene (essential-oil) preparation, taken as capsules or tablets, used for kidney and ureter stones. Blends contain different oils, so these data do not apply equally to every blend. Serious harms: a 2012 systematic review of 42 case reports and case series found 71 patients with adverse effects of aromatherapy, ranging from mild to severe and including one death (the abstract does not say how the oil was used or which oil was involved in the death); dermatitis was the most common, lavender, peppermint, tea tree and ylang-ylang oils were most often responsible, and the authors say aromatherapy can cause adverse effects, some of them serious, whose frequency is unknown. Swallowed: a 2005 case report describes fulminant liver failure in a 15-month-old boy after he swallowed clove oil (the abstract does not say how he came to swallow it); his liver impairment resolved after intravenous N-acetylcysteine. The authors say clove oil has important liver-toxic effects, and their analysis of a national database found a 14-fold rise in home accidents related to aromatherapy from 1994 to 1999. Applied to the skin: in a study of 8 children with atopic eczema, alongside normal medical treatment, children were randomly allocated to massage with a mixture of essential oils, and a control group had massage without them; both groups improved, with no significant difference between them. In further study of the essential-oil group, the eczema got worse after two further 8-week periods of therapy (the abstract describes no comparison group for these periods); the authors say this may have been because the treatment's novelty wore off, or strongly suggests possible allergic contact dermatitis caused by the oils themselves, and warn that short-term benefits could be overturned by adverse effects after repeated use. A case report describes allergic contact dermatitis in a 39-year-old woman who had used aromatherapy products for 2 to 3 years and had a red rash on her face and chest; the abstract does not say how the products were used; patch tests were positive to fragrance mix (and to neomycin), and the rash cleared quickly when she stopped the products. In patch-test data from a network of dermatology departments (2010 to 2019), 908 of 10,930 dermatitis patients (8.3%) tested with 12 essential oils "in an aimed manner" (the abstract does not say how patients were chosen for testing) reacted to at least one, most often ylang-ylang, lemongrass, jasmine, sandalwood, clove and neroli oils; the authors say sensitisation occurs, though infrequently in most cases, and that masseurs and cosmeticians have an increased risk. Breast growth in children (case reports, disputed): a 2007 report describes breast growth in three prepubertal boys that coincided with skin products containing lavender and tea tree oils and went away soon after the products were stopped, and its authors conclude that repeated skin exposure to these oils probably caused it; a 2019 report describes three prepubertal girls and one boy with signs of oestrogen action and continuous exposure to lavender-containing fragrances, whose breast growth went away when the products were stopped. A 2020 systematic review of 11 such cases found the reporting insufficient, no evidence for a link with tea tree oil and little to no evidence for a link with lavender oil; in a 2022 cross-sectional survey of parents of 556 children, no cases of breast growth in prepubertal boys were found in either the exposed or the unexposed group, and the total risk of endocrine disorders was 1.94% in children exposed to lavender or tea tree oil products and 0.69% in those not exposed, a difference that was not statistically significant (risk ratio 2.8, 95% CI 0.35 to 22.2); the authors conclude that regularly exposed children had the same risk as those not exposed; and a 2023 review says it cannot be concluded that the oils caused these effects. These cases concern lavender- or tea-tree-containing skin products and fragrances, not the blends tested on the condition pages. In the 86-person trial of a thyme, rosemary, lavender and cedarwood blend massaged into the scalp for alopecia areata, the authors called the treatment safe, but the abstract does not list adverse events; a systematic review of complementary therapies for alopecia areata, which included essential-oil aromatherapy, found adverse events rare and mild for all the therapies it evaluated. No adverse-event data were found in the abstracts of the abdominal-massage trials for period pain cited on the pages. Inhaled: the 8-person pilot study of lavender or cypress aroma oil during sleep in people with sleep apnoea gives no safety data. A case report describes allergic airborne contact dermatitis, relapsing eczema on uncovered skin, particularly the scalp, neck and hands, in a 53-year-old patient after a year-long use of aroma lamps, with patch-test allergy to lavender, jasmine and rosewood among other oils; the skin cleared with steroid treatment on the skin and by mouth, and the authors considered complete renewal of the interior of the patient's flat essential because the oils persisted in the home. Case reports also describe acute eosinophilic pneumonia (an inflammation of the lungs) in a Japanese woman who had started aromatherapy with essential oil in a humidifier two weeks earlier, diagnosed as caused by inhaling the oil and resolving after steroid treatment, and, in a 72-year-old man with progressive shortness of breath, exogenous lipoid pneumonia (lung inflammation from inhaled oil) that mimicked a tumour and was attributed to essential oils inhaled from a commercially available breath-freshening spray. No adverse-event data were found for the essential-oil spray or gargle used for snoring itself; the lipoid pneumonia case above involved a different, breath-freshening spray. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
